newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ growth target would lead to higher rates - NBNZ.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ growth target would lead to higher rates - NBNZ.

text.p: Explicitly adding economic growth to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's goal could result in higher interest rates, the National Bank of New Zealand said on Thursday.
The bank said there was a risk that adding growth would cloud the RBNZ's operations and reduce its credibility, and higher rates would result.

NBNZ economists used the "Taylor Rule", designed by prominent U.S. economist John Taylor, to assess the impact on current monetary policy settings of incorporating growth in to the RBNZ's objectives, widening the inflation target from its
current 0-2 percent, and raising the target's mid point.
The rule takes explicit note of inflation and economic growth to decide an appropriate interest rate setting, but makes no explicit account of the exchange rate.

The economists' results suggested adding growth to the RBNZ's objective may make little difference to current interest rates, and widening the target band would make limited difference providing the mid-point stayed at one percent.
A higher inflation target would, at best, only temporarily reduce short term interest rates, and possibly lead to higher rates over time, the economists said.

Chief economist Adrian Orr said the Taylor Rule and the RBNZ's economic forecasts suggested interest rates were poised to decline over 1997. However, he warned this assumed no significant policy change, and a sharp fiscal expansion would alter the picture.
The Taylor Rule is based on two elements. One decides a "neutral" short term interest rate that is neither expansionary nor contractionary.

The other sets a "policy rule" consistent with achieving low inflation and stabilising output growth. A predetermined percentage amount is added or subtracted to interest rates depending on how much inflation and GDP fall above or below target levels.

NBNZ said the Taylor Rule can be used to mimic past monetary policy and assess where short-term interest rates should currently be. The economists said the resulting "neutral" real short rate was 6.9 percent, and added that the rule suggested interest rates were about right over the September quarter, at around 10 percent.

They cautioned that the rule made little allowance for different speeds at which interest rates may impact on the economy during the business cycle. It also ignored the nature of economic shocks, was reactive and ignored other information.
Despite its simplicity, however, the rule provided several insights. It mimicked other central banks' behaviour well, suggesting the RBNZ's policy was not unique as often suggested.
"Instead, NZ's advantage is the clarity of the RB's single inflation goal. This removes the temptation for short-term political tinkering," the economists said.
